title: As a game developer, the engine ships a modern production 3D renderer — PBR materials, global illumination or baked lighting, shadows, post-processing
As a game developer, 2D is a first-class workflow — sprites, tilemaps, 2D physics — not a 3D afterthought
As a game developer, built-in physics — rigid bodies, collisions, raycasts — works out of the box
As a game developer, I can profile and scale — a real profiler, plus data-oriented paths (ECS, jobs, instancing) when scenes get heavy
As a game developer, the primary scripting language is productive and fully exposes the engine API, with a debugger behind it
As a technical artist, I can build gameplay logic with visual scripting without writing code
As a game developer, the edit-run loop is fast — hot reload or near-instant preview after a script change
As a technical artist, a full visual editor — viewport, inspector, prefabs/scene composition — is the primary way to build levels
As a game developer, I can extend and automate the editor itself — custom tools, editor scripts, plugins that manipulate scenes and assets programmatically
As a studio lead, the project format and tooling play well with version control and multi-person teams — mergeable scenes, diffable text formats, or built-in collaboration
As a technical artist, asset import is automatable — import hooks, presets, and pipeline scripts process incoming assets without hand-clicking each one
As a game developer, a large asset store or package ecosystem gives me ready-made models, tools, and plugins
As a technical artist, standard interchange formats — glTF, FBX, USD — import cleanly
As a studio lead, one project exports to desktop, mobile, and (directly or via partners) consoles
As a web developer, my game runs in the browser with a reasonable payload — WebGL today, and a credible WebGPU story
As a web developer, the engine installs from a package registry into my existing toolchain — a library I import, bundle, and tree-shake like any dependency
As a game developer, I can build and export the project from the command line, headless, in CI — no human clicking an editor
As a game developer, tests run headlessly — unit and integration tests of game code execute in CI against the real engine
As a game developer, game logic runs headless on servers — a dedicated-server or server-runtime build without rendering
As an AI-native user, an agent can drive the editor and project programmatically — create scenes and nodes, edit properties, trigger builds — through a documented scriptable interface
As an AI-native user, an official AI assistant inside the engine helps with engine tasks — generating scripts, answering API questions, scaffolding scenes or assets
As an AI-native user, LLM-generated code mostly works on the first try — stable, well-documented APIs with abundant public examples the models have seen
As a game developer, I can run ML models inside the game — an official inference runtime for on-device model execution
As a studio lead, the license is permissive with no royalties or per-install fees — I keep what my game earns
As a game developer, I can read and modify the full engine source when I hit a wall
As a studio lead, the pricing and license terms have a track record of stability — no retroactive changes that reprice games already shipped
As a studio lead, the project's governance and funding are transparent — a foundation, published finances, or a public roadmap I can plan against

As an AI-native user, the scripting language has first-class machine tooling — an official language server (LSP) or typed API definitions a coding agent's editor can attach to for completions, diagnostics, and navigation
